what: Albertsons is one of the largest grocery chains in the United States. It operates more than 2,000 supermarkets under about twenty regional names including Safeway, Vons, Jewel-Osco, Acme and Shaw’s, along with pharmacies and fuel stations attached to many of them.
customers: Grocery shoppers across much of the United States, with the regional brand names deliberately retained because local recognition matters more than a national identity in food retail.
money: Food sold through supermarkets, including own-brand products at higher margins.
Prescriptions and health products in in-store pharmacies.
Petrol stations attached to stores and other revenue.
moat: Grocery is a scale business with very thin margins where cost per unit distributed decides who survives. Albertsons’ advantages are its regional brand strength, its own-brand products which carry better margins than national brands, and its pharmacies, which bring customers in far more frequently than groceries alone.
risks: A trailing net loss of $51.3M on $83.2B of revenue shows how little margin there is to absorb anything going wrong.
Debt of $15.3B against $198.6M of cash is very heavy, much of it lease obligations, and it dominates the equity value.
The failed merger with Kroger consumed years of management attention and left the company without the scale it sought.
Walmart, Costco and Amazon all compete on price with cost structures Albertsons cannot match.
Seventeen analysts average a $14.12 target, about 17% above the current price.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $506.5M on $83.2B of revenue, with the shares at about 11.2 times it and 0.068 times sales.
Revenue has grown every year, from $71.9B in 2022 to $83.2B in 2026.
Groceries are the most recession-resistant retail category there is, because people buy food in every economy.
Pharmacies drive visit frequency and loyalty well beyond what food shopping alone would produce.
Own-brand products carry higher margins than national brands and have been growing as a share of sales.
watch: Identical-store sales excluding fuel, and gross margin. In grocery, a tenth of a percentage point of margin on $83 billion is the entire profit, so the margin line is the business.
view: Grocery retailing is a business of almost unimaginable thinness, and the Albertsons numbers show it starkly: $83 billion of revenue and a trailing net loss of $51 million. That is not a bad year so much as a demonstration of the structure — a tenth of a percentage point of gross margin on $83 billion is roughly the entire annual profit, which means the margin line is not a metric here, it is the whole business.

Albertsons’ position within that structure is awkward. It is large enough to have scale but not large enough to match Walmart or Costco on cost, and those two compete on price with structural advantages Albertsons cannot replicate. The failed Kroger merger was an attempt to fix exactly this, and its collapse left the company having spent years of management attention to end up where it started, with the same scale problem and a shareholder base that had priced in a deal.

What the company does have is better than it appears. Its regional brands — Safeway, Vons, Jewel-Osco, Acme — carry genuine local loyalty, which is why they were never consolidated into one national name. Pharmacies bring customers in at a frequency groceries alone could not justify, and a pharmacy customer is far stickier than a shopper comparing prices. Own-brand products earn more than national brands and have been growing. None of this beats Walmart on price, but it does give Albertsons a reason to exist alongside it.

The problem that overshadows everything is $15.3 billion of debt against $198 million of cash. Much of it is lease obligations, which are genuinely different from borrowed money, but all of it is a fixed claim ahead of shareholders on a business with no margin cushion. At 11.2 times free cash flow the equity is not expensively priced, but it is a thin sliver of value sitting on top of a very large liability, and in that structure small changes in grocery margin produce large changes in what the equity is worth. Identical-store sales and gross margin are the only two numbers worth following.
bull: Own-brand penetration and pharmacy-driven loyalty lift margins modestly, grocery’s recession resistance holds revenue, and $506 million of free cash flow steadily reduces the debt.
bear: Walmart and Costco compress grocery margins further, a sliver of equity sits on $15.3 billion of obligations, and a tenth of a point of margin erases the profit entirely.
